54	
55	\begin{abstract}
56	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) provide powerful pretrained representations, but using them on a downstream task requires attaching a lightweight adapter head. A natural improvement over today's single-head designs is a mixture-of-expert (MoE) adapter that selects a different head for each input window. We show that this natural design catastrophically fails on TSFMs with instance normalization: the router collapses to a single expert and the remaining experts are never used. The cause, which we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, is that instance normalization strips the per-window mean and variance the router needs to distinguish input regimes. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms---load balancing, z-loss, entropy regularization, ReLU routing, and expert-choice---do not recover performance, because the failure is not in the router's optimization but in its input. We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition that yields a signal-ratio predictor of where collapse occurs, including boundary cases where it does not. The fix follows from the diagnosis: \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input. RR-MoA wins on every dataset/freeze-level cell of the primary backbone, generalizes across four further backbones, and is confirmed to be instance-normalization-specific by two negative controls. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox} that we verify empirically: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse, so frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning. A companion architecture (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) restoring raw-signal access at the expert level closes the remaining gap to supervised baselines.
57	\end{abstract}
58	
59	\section{Introduction}
60	\label{sec:intro}
61	
62	Time series foundation models (TSFMs) such as MOMENT~\citep{goswami2024moment}, TimesFM~\citep{das2024timesfm}, Chronos~\citep{ansari2024chronos}, Timer-XL~\citep{liu2025timerxl}, and Moirai~\citep{woo2024moirai} now provide powerful pretrained representations for time series, with several recent variants pushing toward billion-parameter scales~\citep{lee2024units, rasul2024lagllama, shi2024timemoe, ekambaram2024ttm, liu2026timers1}. Using one of these backbones on a downstream task still requires attaching a lightweight adapter head that maps hidden states to predictions, and the design of that adapter---more than the backbone choice---determines deployment utility.
63	
64	Today, every public TSFM benchmark uses a single static head that pools hidden states and projects them to the forecast horizon~\citep{goswami2024moment, das2024timesfm, nie2023patchtst, hu2022lora}. Real time series are not so uniform: ETTh1 mixes quiet baseline segments with sharp seasonal excursions, and a single adapter topology cannot be optimal for every input window. A natural remedy is a \emph{mixture of expert adapters}: a pool of topologically distinct heads with a learned router that assigns each window to the most suitable one. Keeping the backbone frozen while training only the adapter is also what makes deployment practical---one TSFM in GPU memory can serve thousands of tenants through small ($\sim$1.7\,MB) per-task adapters swapped in microseconds, an arrangement that per-dataset models like DLinear~\citep{zeng2023dlinear} cannot match (Appendices~\ref{app:deployment},~\ref{app:benchmark}).
65	
66	This natural mixture-of-experts approach catastrophically fails on TSFMs that use instance normalization. When the standard MoE recipe~\citep{wang2022adamix, fedus2022switch}---routing on hidden states with load balancing---is applied to MOMENT with RevIN, routing entropy drops to zero in most unfrozen configurations (Table~\ref{tab:adamix}). The router learns to send every window to the same expert, and the remaining experts are never used. The mechanism is what we call \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}: RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} strips the per-window mean and variance that the router needs to distinguish input regimes, leaving it with homogenized hidden states. Even with the backbone frozen, hidden-state routing still underperforms; with the backbone unfrozen, the dominant expert receives larger gradients which reshape the backbone to serve it even more, closing a co-adaptation feedback loop within tens of training steps (Figure~\ref{fig:trajectory}). The failure is specific to instance normalization: backbones such as Moirai that use LayerNorm instead of RevIN do not collapse (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}). Standard MoE rescue mechanisms---load balancing, entropy regularization, z-loss, ReLU routing, expert-choice---also do not help (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}), because the problem lies in the router's \emph{input}, not its optimization.
67	
68	Because the diagnosis pinpoints normalization as the cause, the fix principle is direct. \emph{Raw-Routed Mixture of Adapters} (RR-MoA) routes on the raw, pre-normalization input $\mathbf{X}_\text{raw}$ while keeping the backbone strictly frozen; only the router and five canonical expert heads are trainable. The same principle predicts a \emph{Frozen Paradox}: unfreezing triggers co-adaptation collapse (Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen}), so frozen adapters should beat full fine-tuning, which we confirm empirically.
69	
70	\paragraph{Contributions.}
71	\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em, itemsep=0.15em, topsep=0.2em]
72	\item We identify \emph{normalization-induced routing collapse}, a failure mode of MoE adapters on TSFMs that is distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE-rescue literature, and isolate it through eight converging causal controls.
73	\item We formalize the mechanism through a mutual-information decomposition (Observation~\ref{thm:mi_decomp}) that yields a signal-ratio predictor of which datasets benefit from raw routing---including boundary cases where they do not---and validate the same principle across three normalization families, five backbones, and a vision modality.
74	\item We propose RR-MoA, a minimal architectural fix that routes on raw pre-normalization input, and a companion variant (Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+}) that restores raw-signal access at the expert level. Together they close the gap to per-dataset supervised baselines while preserving frozen-backbone deployability.
75	\end{itemize}
76	
77	\section{Related Work}
78	
79	\textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.
80	
81	\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. These designs place experts inside the backbone architecture. RR-MoA instead applies MoE at the \emph{adapter level} on a frozen backbone---an orthogonal design axis. We validate that the two axes stack: RR-MoA on top of Moirai-MoE still yields $-37\%$ MSE (\S\ref{sec:cross_backbone}, Table~\ref{tab:moirai_moe}).
82	
83	\textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.
84	
85	{\looseness=-1 \textbf{Normalization in Time Series.} RevIN~\citep{kim2021revin} mitigates distribution shift; DishTS~\citep{fan2023dishts} and Non-stationary Transformers~\citep{liu2022nonstationary} partially recover stripped statistics. Concurrently, \citet{berthelier2026revin} independently show that several RevIN components are redundant or detrimental, and \citet{zou2025ibnorm} argue that variance-centric normalization (BatchNorm, LayerNorm, RMSNorm) is suboptimal for representation learning because two representations with identical mean and variance can encode different amounts of task-relevant information. We identify a specific, mechanistic consequence of this principle that has not been characterized in the MoE literature: when the stripped statistics carry the \emph{routing} signal in a downstream MoE adapter, instance normalization causes catastrophic routing collapse---a failure mode distinct from the optimization-induced collapse studied in standard MoE rescue literature.}
86	
87	\textbf{NAS and LLM-Guided Search.} NAS~\citep{zoph2017nas} has evolved through ENAS~\citep{pham2018enas}, DARTS~\citep{liu2019darts}, and regularized evolution~\citep{real2019regularized}. Shears~\citep{munoz2024shears} and RZ-NAS~\citep{ji2025rznas} search adapter hyperparameters for LLMs; NAS-LoRA~\citep{chen2025naslora} targets vision adapters. FunSearch~\citep{romera2024funsearch}, EvoPrompting~\citep{chen2023evoprompting}, PartEvo~\citep{hu2025partevo}, and ReEvo~\citep{ye2024reevo} demonstrate LLM-guided program synthesis. We use this paradigm for expert pool construction (Appendix~\ref{app:aas_details}).
88

90	\label{sec:method}

input.new_string:
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not work, and the reason is structural rather than algorithmic: the normalization layer the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics that a downstream router would have used to tell input regimes apart. Once that is recognized, every part of the empirical picture follows. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms cannot help, because they target the router's optimization rather than its input. Hidden-state routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones. Frozen-backbone adapters beat full fine-tuning, because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback. input.old_string: \textbf{TSFM Adaptation.} The standard approach to adapting a frozen TSFM is to attach a lightweight module---LoRA~\citep{hu2022lora}, bottleneck adapters~\citep{houlsby2019adapters}, or a linear probe~\citep{goswami2024moment}---and tune it on downstream data. Recent work has expanded the design space: MSFT~\citep{qiao2025msft} proposes multi-scale finetuning, TRACE~\citep{li2025trace} introduces importance-based LoRA selection with reconstructed heads, and AdaPTS~\citep{benechehab2025adapts} adapts input representations rather than the backbone itself. Beyond LoRA~\citep{gupta2024beyondlora} surveys PEFT alternatives for Chronos; Prune-then-Finetune~\citep{zhao2025prune} applies structured pruning; in-context fine-tuning~\citep{faw2025icf} adapts at inference time. TEMPLATE~\citep{zhang2025template} and GIFT-Eval~\citep{woo2024gifteval} address model selection and benchmarking. All of these search over finetuning \textit{strategies}---learning rates, rank, which layers to tune---rather than the adapter \textit{architecture} itself. Our work addresses this gap: we show that the choice of adapter topology should be \emph{per-sample}, not per-dataset.

\textbf{MoE in Foundation Models.} Mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing~\citep{fedus2022switch} has been applied \emph{within} TSFM backbones to scale model capacity: Moirai-MoE~\citep{liu2025moiraimoe} routes frequency bands across internal experts, and Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe} uses sparse activation to reach billions of parameters. \textbf{MoE routing collapse and rescue.} Routing collapse---where a few experts capture all traffic---is a well-known failure mode in MoE training. Existing solutions attack it from the \emph{optimization side}: load-balancing losses~\citep{fedus2022switch}, z-loss~\citep{zoph2022stmoe}, Expert-Choice routing~\citep{zhou2022expertchoice}, and ReLU gating~\citep{zhang2025remoe}. AdaMix~\citep{wang2022adamix} brings MoE to adapter fine-tuning in NLP but still routes on hidden states. All of these enforce diversity through training objectives without asking whether the router's \emph{input} contains discriminative information in the first place. We sweep all five families across eleven configurations on MOMENT$+$RevIN and show \textbf{none recover MSE to within $2.7{\times}$ of RR-MoA} (Table~\ref{tab:rescue}). Our contribution is complementary: we show that when normalization structurally removes routing information from hidden states, no configuration from any of the five standard rescue families can compensate. Concurrently, recent work in NLP and vision has moved toward eliminating external routers entirely: AoE~\citep{lv2025aoe} lets experts self-select via activation norms, ERMoE~\citep{cheng2025ermoe} routes via cosine similarity to learned eigenbases (achieving 0\% collapse), and Routing-Free MoE~\citep{liu2026routingfree} encapsulates gating within each expert. We validate this self-routing principle in our setting (\S\ref{sec:main_results}): self-gated experts on raw input match RR-MoA, while the same architecture on hidden states collapses---confirming the bottleneck is normalization, not router design. Concurrent theoretical work~\citep{wang2026myth} proves MoE specialization reflects hidden-state geometry: tokens with similar hidden states activate similar experts. We extend this one step upstream by identifying what \emph{shapes} that geometry on TSFMs---instance normalization homogenizes hidden states by stripping per-window statistics, producing the geometric collapse that geometry-based analyses describe but do not causally explain.

The bound is empirically tight on our datasets. Estimating the leakage with CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated to within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}, so the result holds beyond Gaussianity. Direct measurement of $H(E \mid S)$ via a held-out classifier shows that normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of the routing entropy, and the bound (ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). As an independent check, training the normalization strength $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). Notably, $H(E \mid S)$ alone does \emph{not} correlate with the empirical raw-routing benefit ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$), while $R(\mathcal{D})$ does ($\rho{=}{-}0.88$, Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}): what matters is the routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics, not the MI loss.

Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio} reports the validation in detail. The Spearman rank correlation between $R(\mathcal{D})$ and the MSE improvement $\Delta\%$ from raw routing is $\rho = -0.88$ ($p < 0.002$; bootstrap CI $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$): datasets where normalization strips more routing signal benefit more from bypassing it. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case ($\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$). Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier; the Conv1d router exploits temporal shape patterns beyond location-scale, consistent with the SSR ablation ($+43\%$ degradation). Additional ablations (SSR, RDGF, per-quartile analysis) are in Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}.

Sparse routing and task generalization. Top-2 sparse routing adds 4.3 ms (+10%) while retaining
63% of the dense gain; scaling K=3→20 changes MSE by <5% (Appendix I). RR-MoA generalizes
to imputation (7/8 datasets; Appendix J).
Multi-horizon generalization. RR-MoA wins 24/24 configurations across H∈{96, 192, 336, 720}
on ETTh1, ETTm1, and Weather (5 seeds each; Table A1), with improvements of 27–49% over
the best fixed adapter at every horizon. The advantage is stable across horizon length: at H=720,
RR-MoA still improves by 27–41%. Residual-IA+ (Appendix R.1, Figure R5) further extends this to
all 6 datasets across 5 backbones and 4 horizons (Table R33).

5   Conclusion
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not
work, and the reason is structural rather than algorithmic: the normalization layer the backbone relies
on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics that a downstream router would have used
to distinguish input regimes. Once that is recognized, the empirical picture follows. Standard MoE
rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-state
routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones; frozen
adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback; and the
simplest fix—routing on the raw, pre-normalization input—wins consistently across datasets, freeze
levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio statistic
predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises beyond
MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA+ that restore raw-signal access at the expert level. We see
RR-MoA less as a new architecture than as the minimal architectural concession the diagnosis forces.
Limitations. Our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five rescue families
that dominate current MoE practice; whether other schemes (e.g., the FFN-internal experts of Time-
MoE [15]) exhibit the same failure mode is open. The signal ratio R(D) uses first and second
moments only and can miss higher-order routing signals (Solar in our suite). Proposition 1 is proved
for linear backbones; the trajectory experiments confirm the mechanism in full Transformers but the
formal extension is left to future work.

5   Conclusion
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not
work, and the reason is structural rather than algorithmic: the normalization layer the backbone relies
on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics that a downstream router would have used
to distinguish input regimes. Once that is recognized, the empirical picture follows. Standard MoE
rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-state
routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones; frozen
adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback; and the
simplest fix—routing on the raw, pre-normalization input—wins consistently across datasets, freeze
levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio statistic
predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises beyond
MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA+ that restore raw-signal access at the expert level. We see
RR-MoA less as a new architecture than as the minimal architectural concession the diagnosis forces.
Limitations. Our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five rescue families

Two limiting cases are worth naming. If the router's signal lies entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$---RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution in nats. At the opposite extreme, if $(M,\Sigma)$ carries no expert-relevant information, the loss is zero. Real datasets fall in between, with the loss bounded above by the variance the stripped statistics contribute to $X$. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for how much potential routing information the stripped statistics could carry; it is not an estimate of the MI loss itself, but it is what we can compute on every dataset, and we use it to predict where raw routing will help. Full proof and a rate-distortion interpretation are in Appendices~\ref{app:proofs}, \ref{app:prop2_depth}.

The bound is empirically tight. CCA estimates $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated to within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by the KSG estimator~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of the routing entropy and the bound (ii) gap averages $0.075$ nats ($4.7\%$ of $\log K$; Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). Independently, training the normalization strength $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). The signal ratio $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts the empirical raw-routing benefit at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$; bootstrap CI $[-1.00, -0.51]$; $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}), while $H(E \mid S)$ alone does not ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$): what matters for raw-routing benefit is the routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics, not the MI loss itself. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case; Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier, where the Conv1d router exploits shape patterns beyond location-scale (SSR ablation: $+43\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).

A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not work, and the reason is structural: the normalization the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs to distinguish input regimes. Once that is recognized, the empirical picture follows. Standard MoE rescue mechanisms target the router's optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-state routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones; frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback; and the simplest fix---routing on the raw, pre-normalization input---wins consistently across datasets, freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio statistic predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises beyond MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA\textsuperscript{+} that restore raw-signal access at the expert level.

\textbf{Limitations.} Our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five rescue families that dominate current MoE practice; whether other schemes (e.g., FFN-internal experts of Time-MoE~\citep{shi2024timemoe}) exhibit the same failure mode is open. $R(\mathcal{D})$ uses first and second moments only and can miss higher-order routing signals (Solar in our suite). Proposition~\ref{prop:frozen} is proved for linear backbones; the formal extension to full Transformers is left to future work.

492	Two limiting cases pin down the bound. If the router's signal lives entirely in the stripped statistics ($E \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid (M,\Sigma)$), the bound saturates and $I(X; E) - I(S; E) = H(E)$---RevIN destroys the entire routing distribution. If $(M,\Sigma)$ carries no expert-relevant information, the loss is zero. Real datasets fall in between, and the loss is bounded by the variance the stripped statistics contribute to $X$. We therefore use the \emph{signal ratio} $R(\mathcal{D}) = [\mathrm{Var}(M) + \mathrm{Var}(\Sigma)] / \overline{\mathrm{Var}(S)}$ as a tractable monotone proxy for that variance contribution---computable on every dataset, used to predict where raw routing will help. Full proof in Appendices~\ref{app:proofs}, \ref{app:prop2_depth}.
493	
494	The bound is empirically tight: CCA gives $\varepsilon \in [0.09, 1.26]$ nats, cross-validated within ${\pm}0.26$ nats by KSG~\citep{kraskov2004ksg}; a held-out classifier shows normalization retains only $16$--$41\%$ of the routing entropy with bound (ii) gap averaging $0.075$ nats (Appendix~\ref{app:mi_tightness}). Training $\alpha \in [0,1]$ as a learnable parameter, gradient descent converges to $\alpha < 0.5$ on all six datasets ($30/30$ runs; Appendix~\ref{app:learnable_alpha}). $R(\mathcal{D})$ predicts the raw-routing benefit at Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.88$ ($p{<}0.002$, $n{=}9$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_ratio}), while $H(E \mid S)$ alone does not ($\rho{=}{-}0.12$): routing \emph{potential} in the stripped statistics matters, not the MI loss itself. Traffic ($R{=}0.14$, $\Delta{=}{+}2.9\%$) is correctly predicted as a boundary case; Solar ($R{=}0.06$) is the one outlier (SSR ablation $+43\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:routing_ablations}).

5   Conclusion
A natural mixture-of-expert adapter for instance-normalized time series foundation models does not
work, and the reason is structural: the normalization the backbone relies on for distribution shift also
strips the per-window statistics a downstream router needs to distinguish input regimes. Standard
MoE rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot help; hidden-
state routing collapses on instance-normalized backbones but not on LayerNorm or T5-style ones;
frozen adapters beat full fine-tuning because unfreezing only deepens the co-adaptation feedback;
the simplest fix—routing on the raw, pre-normalization input—wins consistently across datasets,
freeze levels, backbones, and modalities. The diagnosis is also actionable: a tractable signal-ratio
statistic predicts which datasets benefit without training any model, and the same principle generalises
beyond MoE adapters to choices like Residual-IA+ that restore raw-signal access at the expert level.
Limitations: our analysis covers RevIN-style instance normalization and the five dominant rescue
families; whether other schemes (e.g., Time-MoE [15]’s FFN-internal experts) exhibit the same
failure mode is open; R(D) uses second-order moments and can miss higher-order routing signals
(Solar in our suite); Proposition 1 is proved for linear backbones, with the formal extension to full
Transformers left to future work.

References
 [1] Ashish Vaswani, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez,

5   Conclusion
A natural MoE adapter on instance-normalized TSFMs fails for structural reasons: the normalization
the backbone relies on for distribution shift also strips the per-window statistics a downstream router
needs. Standard rescue mechanisms target the router’s optimization rather than its input and cannot
help; routing on the raw, pre-normalization input does, and the same principle predicts the Frozen
Paradox and motivates Residual-IA+ . The signal-ratio statistic identifies where the fix applies without
training. Limitations: we cover RevIN-style normalization and the five dominant rescue families;
R(D) uses second-order moments and can miss higher-order signals (Solar); Proposition 1 is proved
for linear backbones, with the Transformer extension left to future work.

\textbf{Why RevIN destroys routing: formal analysis.} The experiments above converge on a single mechanism: instance normalization strips the per-window statistics that the router uses to tell input regimes apart. To pin this down, we ask what information the router actually has access to before and after normalization. Each input window $\mathbf{x}_i$ decomposes into a mean $M_i = \mu(\mathbf{x}_i)$, a scale $\Sigma_i = \sigma(\mathbf{x}_i)$, and a shape $\mathbf{S}_i = (\mathbf{x}_i - M_i)/\Sigma_i$. RevIN maps $\mathbf{x}_i \mapsto \mathbf{S}_i$ and discards $(M_i, \Sigma_i)$, so the question reduces to how much routing information lives in the discarded part. The mutual-information chain rule gives a clean answer.
